description:
## Overview

The SVC_$ subsystem implements Domain/OS syscall dispatching via M68K TRAP instructions.
Each TRAP number corresponds to a different argument count for syscall validation.

## Completed Work

- **TRAP #0** (0 args): `domain_os/svc/sau2/trap0.s` - Simple syscalls, no argument validation
- **TRAP #1** (1 arg): `domain_os/svc/sau2/trap1.s` - Validates USP + 1 arg, 66 entries at 0xe7b05c
- **TRAP #2** (2 args): `domain_os/svc/sau2/trap2.s` - Validates USP + 2 args, 133 entries at 0xe7b094
- **TRAP #3** (3 args): `domain_os/svc/sau2/trap3.s` - Validates USP + 3 args, 155 entries at 0xe7b0d8
- **TRAP #4** (4 args): `domain_os/svc/sau2/trap4.s` - Validates USP + 4 args, 131 entries at 0xe7b120
- **TRAP #5** (5 args): `domain_os/svc/sau2/trap5.s` - Complex syscalls, validates USP + 5 args, 99 entries
- **TRAP #6** - Not used for SVC calls (points to FIM_$UNDEF_TRAP)
- **TRAP #7** (6 args): `domain_os/svc/sau2/trap7.s` - Validates USP + 6 args, 59 entries at 0xe7b1d8
- **TRAP #8** (variable args): `domain_os/svc/sau2/trap8.s` - Variable-argument dispatcher, uses argcount lookup table, 56 entries at 0xe7b240
- **Shared tables**: `domain_os/svc/svc_tables.c` - C code, shared across SAUs
- **Header**: `domain_os/svc/svc.h` - Constants, syscall numbers, table declarations

## TRAP Numbering Note

TRAP #6 is NOT used for SVC dispatching - it points to FIM_$UNDEF_TRAP which generates a fault. The naming convention follows the actual M68K TRAP instruction numbers:
- SVC_$TRAP0-5: Handle M68K TRAP #0-5
- SVC_$TRAP7: Handles M68K TRAP #7 (6-arg syscalls)
- SVC_$TRAP8: Handles M68K TRAP #8 (variable-arg syscalls)

All SVC TRAP dispatchers are now complete.
close_reason: All SVC TRAP dispatchers (0-5, 7-8) implemented. Corrected naming: TRAP #6 is unused, TRAP #7 handles 6-arg syscalls, TRAP #8 handles variable-arg syscalls.

title: TTY: confirm historical names for char classes 0x05/0x06 (XON vs XOFF)
description: tty/tty.h: class 0x05 (0xE1BA42) sets TTY_STATUS_XON_XOFF and calls the xon/xoff handler with TRUE; class 0x06 (0xE1BA60) clears it, calls with FALSE and advances the output EC.  That reads as 0x05=stop-output(^S) and 0x06=resume(^Q), i.e. the reverse of the current TTY_CHAR_CLASS_XON/XOFF names.  Confirm against TTY_$I_SET_DFL_FUNCS' default table (0xE6720E) before renaming.  TODO comment is in tty/tty.h.
close_reason: Resolved from the two default tables plus the handlers. TTY_$I_INIT (0x00E33284) copies the default function characters from 0x00E351D8 (labelled tty_$i_dfl_func_chars); TTY_$I_SET_DFL_FUNCS (0x00E67274) sets A5=0x00E8242C whose first 18 words are the function-index -> char-class table (tty_$i_dfl_func_classes), with the enable mask 0x0001FFFF at 0x00E82450. Function index 13 = char 0x13 (^S, DC3 = XOFF) -> class 0x05; index 14 = char 0x11 (^Q, DC1 = XON) -> class 0x06. That matches the handlers: class 0x05 (0x00E1BA42) bset.b #2,(0x9,A2) and calls the handler with st (TRUE); class 0x06 (0x00E1BA60) bclr.b #2 and calls with clr.w (FALSE) then advances the output EC. tty_$i_put_chars returns 0 while bit 2 is set (0x00E1B032). So the old names were reversed. Renamed TTY_CHAR_CLASS_XOFF=0x05, TTY_CHAR_CLASS_XON=0x06 and TTY_STATUS_XON_XOFF -> TTY_STATUS_OUTPUT_STOPPED; fixed tty/tty.h, tty/i_rcv.c, tty/i_put_chars.c and both tty tests. description: proc2/fork.c: at 0x00E72CC6 the error is written to *status_ret, then the jump to 0x00E73240 exits via 0x00E732D6 which overwrites *status_ret with the A6-0x2C local, never written on that path. Reproduced faithfully; confirm against a second Domain/OS build whether this is a genuine original bug.
close_reason: CONFIRMED an original bug; reproduced, not repaired. Traced every reference to A6-0x2C in the 1814-byte PROC2_$FORK: writes come only from callees handed 'pea (-0x2c,A6)' at 0x00E72D02 (PROC1_$ALLOC_STACK), 0x00E72D46 (PROC1_$BIND), 0x00E72E60 (EC2_$REGISTER_EC1), 0x00E72EA6 (ACL_$ALLOC_ASID), 0x00E72EB6 (AUDIT_$INHERIT_AUDIT), 0x00E72F0E (FILE_$FORK_LOCK), 0x00E72F4A (MST_$FORK), 0x00E72F6E and 0x00E72FA0 (MST_$GET_VA_INFO), 0x00E730FE (PROC1_$RESUME), plus 'bset.b #0x7,(-0x2c,A6)' at 0x00E731B8; reads are at 0x00E73114 (CRASH_SYSTEM) and 0x00E732D6. The MST_$ALLOC_ASID failure branch is taken at 0x00E72CC6, sets bit 31 of the CALLER's status at 0x00E72CC8, then 'bra.w 0x00E73240' at 0x00E72CCC. Every store listed above lies strictly between 0x00E72CCC and 0x00E73240; the range 0x00E73240..0x00E732D4 contains no reference to A6-0x2C at all; and nothing before 0x00E72CCC touches it (the only frame store in 0x00E72BCE..0x00E72CCC is (-0x20,A6) for TIME_$CLOCK). So 0x00E732D6 'move.l (-0x2c,A6),(A2)' hands the caller the previous frame's leftover and discards the real error. That the author knew the difference is visible at 0x00E72C2E, where the 'table full' exit branches to 0x00E732DA, deliberately past that store. No second Domain/OS build to diff against, so the conclusion is documented in proc2/fork.c (a 30-line note on the 'status' declaration plus a note at the branch), in Ghidra (EOL comments at 0x00E72CCC and 0x00E732D6, decompiler comment at 0x00E72CC6), and covered by proc2/test/test_fork.c::test_alloc_asid_failure_goes_to_entry_teardown, which asserts the branch reaches cleanup_entry (0x00E73240) and not cleanup_locked (0x00E73146) and does not assert the indeterminate status.

title: Revisit CPU architecture vs SAU vs feature-level code organization
description:
The current code organization uses SAU (System Architecture Unit) numbers for platform-specific code splits (e.g., ec/sau2/advance.s). However, this conflates several different concerns:

1. **CPU architecture** (m68k vs x86 vs ARM) - instruction set, calling conventions, register usage
2. **SAU variants** (sau1, sau2, etc.) - Apollo-specific hardware configurations
3. **Feature-level differences** - e.g., MMU type, peripheral support

The ec/sau2/*.s files contain m68k assembly for SR (Status Register) manipulation to disable/enable interrupts. This is fundamentally a CPU architecture concern, not an SAU-level concern - the same code would work on any m68k-based SAU.

Consider reorganizing to something like:
- `ec/arch/m68k/` for m68k-specific assembly
- `ec/arch/x86/` for x86 equivalents (when porting)
- Keep SAU-level splits only for actual hardware variant differences

This would make the retargetability goal clearer and avoid confusion about what each directory level represents.

title: CAL_$WRITE_CALENDAR writes the MSM5832 leap bit at D10 bit 3, TIME_$READ_CAL uses bit 2
description: cal/write_calendar.c 0x00E816D6 does 'add.w #0x50,D1w' on the day before splitting it into tens/ones, which sets bit 3 of the D10 (date tens) register.  TIME_$READ_CAL sets the leap flag with 'bset.l #2' (0x00E2AE78) and masks the date tens with 3 (0x00E2AEC8), i.e. bit 2 - which is where the MSM5832 datasheet puts the leap-year bit.  The 0x50 looks like the 24-hour-select idiom used for the hour (0x00E816EA, H10 bit 3) applied to the wrong register.  Both sides are reproduced faithfully in C with a TODO comment in cal/write_calendar.c; this bead tracks confirming the hardware behaviour (MSM5832 datasheet / a second SAU image) before deciding whether it is an original bug.
close_reason: Confirmed an original bug in the writer; both sides left reproduced as found. MSM5832 D10 (address 8) is {D0,D1 = date tens, D2 = leap year, D3 = unused}; H10 (address 5) is {D0,D1 = hour tens, D2 = PM, D3 = 24-hour select}. Both routines compute the SAME leap predicate -- (year mod 100 + (month > 2)) mod 4 == 0 (writer 0x00E816C0..0x00E816D4; reader 0x00E2AE60..0x00E2AE72, where the -0x51/+0x64 and the +1 cancel the 80) -- but deposit it in different bits. TIME_$READ_CAL uses bset.l #2 (0x00E2AE78) = D10 bit 2 and masks the date tens with 3 (0x00E2AEC8), which is correct. CAL_$WRITE_CALENDAR does add.w #0x50,D1w (0x00E816D6) before the /10 split; since (v+80)/10 == v/10 + 8 and (v+80)%10 == v%10, that lands in D10 bit 3, the unused bit, so the chip's leap counter is never programmed. The identical add.w #0x50 on the hour (0x00E816EA) IS correct because H10 bit 3 is the 24-hour select -- the idiom was copied onto the wrong register. The correct constant for the date would have been 0x28. Benign in practice: the reader masks D10 with 3 and the chip ignores D3, and TIME_$READ_CAL rewrites D10 with bit 2 set on every read taken in a leap year. Documented in cal/cal.h (resolved note + MSM5832_D10_UNUSED), cal/write_calendar.c and time/read_cal.c; cal/test/test_write_calendar.c now asserts D10 bit 3 set and bit 2 clear. Ghidra EOL comments at 0x00E816D6, 0x00E816EA, 0x00E2AE78, 0x00E2AEC8 and a decompiler comment at 0x00E8167C.

title: CRASH_SYSTEM status constants should be per-module pea(d,PC) cells, not shared globals
description: misc/crash_system.c defines ~22 'status_$t X = 0x...;' globals (Lock_ordering_violation, MMAP_*, Disk_*, ...) that ~70 .c files take the address of and hand to CRASH_SYSTEM.  In the image no such globals exist: every caller does 'pea (d,PC)' to a constant longword inside its own module (see the domain-pascal-codegen-conventions note).  Each constant should become a file-static 'static const status_$t <name>_00eXXXXX = 0x...;' next to its single caller, with the cell address in a comment, and misc/crash_system.h should stop exporting them.  Two entries were only ever inferred rather than read out of the image (Lock_ordering_violation = 0x000A0001 used by ml/lock.c; Disk_Driver_Logic_Err, a duplicate of Disk_driver_logic_err used by disk/dismount.c which also declares it as 'void *').  Lock_order_violation_err was invented and unused and has already been removed.
close_reason: All 22 invented status_$t globals removed from misc/crash_system.c and misc/crash_system.h (and the commented-out block in misc/misc.h, plus the dead externs in ml/ml_internal.h, mst/mst_internal.h, mmap/mmap_internal.h, proc1/proc1_internal.h, ast/ast.h, os/os_internal.h). Every CRASH_SYSTEM call site now has a file-static 'static const status_$t <name>_00eXXXXX' with the cell address in the name; names come from the SR10.4 database (~/src/domainos-archeology/stcodes). 19 distinct cells recovered from the pea (d,PC) at each call: 0x00E20DE4=0x000A0002 proc1_$illegal_lock (ml, shared tail 0x00E20B56); 0x00E30B0C=0x0004000E (mst/init); 0x00E0E1B8=0x00040005 (mst/find); 0x00E3C9FA=0x0008002E (disk/add_que); 0x00E6D130=0x00080022 (disk/dismount); 0x00E1940C=0x00080004 and 0x00E19410=0x00080022 (win); 0x00E0D1C4=0x0006000A, 0x00E0C9E0=0x00060009, 0x00E0D270=0x0006000B, 0x00E0CFF4=0x00060008, 0x00E0CD18=0x00060006, 0x00E0CCB8=0x00060004, 0x00E0D9E6=0x0006000D, 0x00E31B80=0x00060007 (mmap); 0x00E152E0=0x000A0001 (proc1); 0x00E01F18=0x80030003, 0x00E00EAC=0x00050003, 0x00E03544=0x0006000C (ast). The two never-read entries are now read: Lock_ordering_violation was NOT a separate 0x000A0001 -- ML_$LOCK's ordering test (bls.b 0x00E20B56 at 0x00E20AF8) and ML_$UNLOCK's not-locked test (beq.b 0x00E20B56 at 0x00E20BA4) branch into the SAME crash tail, so both use 0x00E20DE4 = 0x000A0002 'illegal lock'; and Disk_Driver_Logic_Err is a genuinely distinct cell at 0x00E6D130 in the disk module (0x00080022), separate from win's 0x00E19410 of the same value. proc1's cell is 0x00E152E0, not the mmap cell the old file claimed. The stale 'void *' / array-typed declarations and the test-local definitions in ml/test/test_exclusion.c and disk/test/test_io.c are gone. All 19 cells labelled in Ghidra, with an EOL comment on the shared ML tail at 0x00E20B56.
